title: Can Prompt Difficulty be Online Predicted for Accelerating RL Finetuning of Reasoning Models?

problem.claim: RL finetuning of reasoning models can require many iterations, frequent prompt evaluations, intensive LLM interactions, and repeated policy updates, causing high computational costs.

gap.claim: Existing online prompt selection methods still rely on exhaustive prompt evaluation and subset selection, which incurs substantial overhead from frequent LLM inference calls.

contributions.claim: The work introduces Model Predictive Prompt Selection (MoPPS), a Bayesian risk-predictive framework for online estimation of prompt difficulty without costly LLM interactions.
MoPPS models prompt success rates as latent variables, performs streaming Bayesian inference, and uses posterior sampling in a constructed multi-armed bandit machine for adaptive prompt selection.
The authors report that implementation code is available online.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments across mathematics, planning, and vision-based geometry tasks reportedly show that MoPPS reliably predicts prompt difficulty.
The authors report that MoPPS accelerates training with significantly reduced LLM rollouts.

narrative_sequence.summary: RL finetuning improves the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
RL optimization can be computationally expensive because it requires repeated evaluations, LLM interactions, and policy updates.
Existing online prompt selection reduces iterations but remains costly because of exhaustive evaluation and frequent inference calls.
MoPPS performs approximate online difficulty prediction using Bayesian inference and posterior sampling for adaptive prompt selection.
The authors report results across mathematics, planning, and vision-based geometry tasks, including reduced LLM rollouts.

source_observation.claim: Prompt selection can be framed as online estimation of prompt difficulty rather than repeated direct evaluation of every prompt.

interpretation.claim: Predictive approximations may reduce expensive model interactions in iterative training pipelines.

application.claim: Use streaming uncertainty-aware estimates and adaptive sampling to prioritize informative training prompts.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish how performance changes across other tasks, model families, or prompt distributions.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify quantitative performance improvements or rollout reductions.
The abstract does not describe baselines, dataset sizes, model configurations, or experimental protocols.
The abstract does not establish independent verification of the reported results.
